title: I Let the Sailing-Club Lifejacket Checkout Catch the Skipper Who Skipped the Log

parts.text: I opened the PFD locker at 8:07 a.m. and two adult jackets were gone with no line on the clipboard. The rule said: SIGN OUT. SIGN IN. SKIPPERS FIRST TO LOG, LAST TO LEAVE. Skipper Mara was already on the dock in a club jacket. I was twenty-eight, crew, holding an empty hook labeled 12. "Skippers are the log." I photographed the empty hook, the clipboard, and her hull number. Then I logged a skip. At 8:14 the harbor master asked why Mara's hull was on an unsigned jacket. I let them finish the sentence they would regret in writing.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The harbor master can see Mara's hull on an unsigned jacket against the clipboard.

social.video_title: The skipper left the dock in an unsigned club jacket — Part 1/2
social.description: Sailing club, an empty hook, and a clipboard she wrote. I logged the skip. Would you have opened the locker?

parts.text: Mara called it a tide until the harbor asked for the log. I printed the skip, the photo, and the clipboard. She signed. Mara last-to-leave like the rule and told crew tides were always about optics. Optics is a word skippers use when a hull exists. Checkout now has a second line: SKIPPERS SIGN. I keep hook 12. Mara initials. The dock finally looks like a club, not a grab. Nobody thanked me, which is how you know a policy finally works. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.

social.description: Skip log, signed jacket, and a second line. Was a tide ever an empty hook?
